title: Bill O'Connor broadcasts and joining Papa Celestin's band
summary: A fan's letter, broadcasting with Bill O'Connor's band, then Celestin sends for him; he stays in Celestin's band from 1934 to 1940-41.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: He kind of hoity so, but he broke his own. And well the people know the Budweiser back and at least they want to sue the Budweiser people. So they backed out. See they had to go back to the front and they pulled out the interciser out of there. And after they played there about a few years, I can show you some words that a fella, we call him Mestedi. I don't know if you know him, he loved dances. A fella, he even reminded me of Mestedi. He used to come and that man would stand inside the band stand and he'd clap all night, so happy. He said, God, you boys, I swear to God, I don't know, that music just does something to me. He went home and I got to the world somewhere and he wrote just what he thought about the band and everything, it was a whole two or three pages, you know. What he thought about the music, you know. And I saw him about a couple of months ago on St. Charles Street, yes, and I played at the band. But why I said that too, I mean, yeah, it was foreign, it turned to be foreign. Well I played there when I, this Bill O'Connor came and got me from there to go to Entertainer's Cabaret, that's on, you know where that was, on the 25th. Franklin Street. Franklin Street, yeah, well that was in the National Army, entertain him. Well I went in there with Bill O'Connor and his riffers. Well that was the first time we broadcast, I was broadcasting with W.H.L. on Mondays. We used to go over there, and the same W.H.L. Williams was out singing with us, you know, everybody used to sing, you know. Well W.H.L. Williams was our vocalist. Understand? And he, first number, the only number, the first number he sang was Moonglow, it must have been Moonglow, you know. And I used to love the way he sang that, yeah. I played that to the entertainer's clothes, in other words, understand? Just about a week or two before they closed, Papa Celestan come for me, sent for me, see, because Heumann had left him to go with Joe Oliver. So Papa Celestan sent him. Herman, which Herman? Herman Franklin. He died, the late Heumann, yeah. Yeah. He died.
The guy used to be with Jimmy Gunn.
Yeah, he lived down in North Roche Blade Street, 1911.
He wrote a nice tune, that tune I'll have him home, and everybody said it, but I never heard

it. He said, like, so, Papa Celestan sent for me. Well, when Papa Celestan, see, I'll consider anybody in your arms, consider when you got a break with Papa Celestan, that was the best band in town, you know. He's going places, see, and I took the offer, and we really, they had a nice fine band. I stayed in that band. I went in that band in 1934, and stayed in Papa's band till 40, 41. Not a lot.
